title: Colons and Semicolons in Lists
keyIdea: A colon can introduce a list, but only after words that make a complete sentence on their own: You will need three things: a torch, a map and a drink. No colon goes straight after a verb such as need, are or held. When the items in a list have commas of their own, such as Paris, France, separate the whole items with semicolons so the reader can see where each one ends, including before the final and. Once you start using semicolons between items, use them all the way through.
familyTip: Write a list together that needs semicolons, such as three friends and where they live (Ava, from Leeds; Sam, from York; and Raj, from Hull). Then read it aloud with only commas and ask: how many people is that now?

visual.caption: Is each list punctuated correctly? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Bring three things: a hat, a coat and gloves.
We visited Rome, Italy; Lima, Peru; and Cairo, Egypt.
The team: Kim, a bowler; Lee, a batter; and Max.
We need: eggs, flour and milk.
Pack three things; a hat, a coat and boots.
My best colours are: red, blue and green.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: decide if a colon fits, turn commas into semicolons, count items, fix slips, build a list.

kid: A colon looks like two dots, one on top of the other. It can open a list. But the words before it must make a whole sentence. You will need three things: a torch, a map and a drink.
Do not put a colon straight after words like need or are. We need eggs and milk is right. We need: eggs and milk is a slip.
Some list items have commas inside them, like Paris, France. Then commas alone get muddled. Put a semicolon between each whole item: Paris, France; Rome, Italy; and Oslo, Norway.
Semicolons help the reader count. I met Sam, my cousin; Ella; and Jo is three people. Once you use a semicolon between items, keep using them to the end.
adult: Ages 10 to 11. The national curriculum in England (English Appendix 2, Year 6) lists the use of the colon to introduce a list and the use of semi-colons within lists, and the Year 5 to 6 writing programme asks pupils to use a wider range of punctuation accurately. These marks build on commas in lists from Year 2.

The test for a list colon is whether the words before it could stand alone as a sentence. You will need the following: passes; We need: does not, because need must run straight on to its object. Semicolons separate list items when one or more items already contain commas, so the reader can see where each item ends. In such a list the semicolon also goes before the final and.

Common mistakes: putting a colon straight after a verb or preposition (are, need, such as, of); using a semicolon to open a list instead of a colon; mixing commas and semicolons between items in the same list; and using semicolons for a short simple list where commas are enough. A careful check is to count the items aloud with the punctuation as written.

In the lab your child decides whether a colon fits six lead-ins and taps the commas in four lists that should become semicolons. They count the items in four lists, find the wrong mark in four sentences and drag a colon and semicolons into three lists to build them from scratch.

practice.prompt: Which sentence uses a colon correctly?
choices: You will need three things: a pen, a ruler and glue.
You will need: a pen, a ruler and glue.
You will: need a pen, a ruler and glue.
practice.hint: Could the words before the colon stand alone as a sentence?
practice.explain: You will need three things is a complete sentence, so the colon fits. You will need is not finished.

practice.prompt: A list has {n} items, and every item has a comma inside it. How many semicolons go between the items?
practice.hint: One semicolon goes in each gap between two whole items.
practice.explain: {n} items have {=n-1} gaps between them, so {=n-1} semicolons, including the one before and.

practice.prompt: Which list needs semicolons between its items?
choices: Leeds, England, Cork, Ireland and Perth, Scotland
apples, pears and plums
red, blue and green
practice.hint: Look for items that have commas inside them.
practice.explain: Leeds, England is one item with a comma inside, so semicolons are needed: Leeds, England; Cork, Ireland; and Perth, Scotland.

practice.prompt: A list has {s} semicolons between its items. How many items are in the list?
practice.hint: Each semicolon sits in a gap between two items.
practice.explain: {s} gaps join {=s+1} items. Commas inside an item do not add more.

practice.prompt: "We saw Rome, Italy; Lima, Peru, and Cairo, Egypt." What should change?
choices: The comma after Peru should be a semicolon.
The comma after Rome should go.
Nothing needs to change.
practice.hint: Once items are split by semicolons, every gap between items needs one.
practice.explain: Lima, Peru; and Cairo, Egypt keeps the semicolons going. The comma after Rome is inside one item and stays.

pool.prompt: What must come before a colon that opens a list?
choices: Words that make a complete sentence
A verb such as need or are
A semicolon
pool.hint: Try reading the words before the colon on their own.
pool.explain: The lead-in must be a complete sentence. A colon straight after need or are cuts the sentence in half.

pool.prompt: Which sentence about the winners is correct?
choices: The winners were Asha and Tom.
The winners were: Asha and Tom.
The winners were; Asha and Tom.
pool.hint: Does were need to run straight on to the names?
pool.explain: were runs straight on to Asha and Tom, so no mark goes there.

pool.prompt: A list has {n} items with commas inside them. How many semicolons does it need?
pool.hint: Count the gaps between whole items, not the items.

pool.prompt: "I met Sam, my cousin; Ella; and Jo." How many people did I meet?
pool.hint: The semicolons show where each person ends.
pool.explain: Sam, my cousin is one person. Then Ella, then Jo: three people.

pool.prompt: Which mark opens a list after a complete sentence?
choices: A colon
A semicolon
A full stop
pool.hint: It looks like two dots, one above the other.
pool.explain: A colon opens the list. Semicolons go between items that have commas inside.

pool.prompt: Why use semicolons in "Ali, aged 9; Ben, aged 10; and Cara, aged 11"?
choices: The items have commas inside them.
To make the list longer.
Semicolons go in every list.
pool.hint: Think about where each item ends.
pool.explain: Each item has a comma inside, so semicolons show where each whole item ends.

pool.prompt: A list of places has {p} items. Each item is a town and its country, like Cork, Ireland. How many commas sit inside the items?
pool.hint: Each item has one comma between its town and country.
pool.explain: One comma inside each of the {p} items makes {p} commas. Semicolons go between the items.

pool.prompt: Which list for a camping trip is punctuated correctly?
choices: Pack three things: a hat, a coat and boots.
Pack three things; a hat, a coat and boots.
Pack: three things, a hat, a coat and boots.
pool.hint: Which mark opens a list after a complete command?
pool.explain: A colon opens the list. A semicolon can't open one, and Pack on its own is not the right lead-in.

pool.prompt: Does "apples, pears and plums" need semicolons?
choices: No: no item has a comma inside.
Yes: every list needs them.
Yes: it has three items.
pool.hint: Semicolons are for items that already have commas.
pool.explain: Simple items only need commas. Semicolons are for items that hold commas of their own.
